<reason>Both sides fought a genuinely clean clash: PRO framed the motion as closing a paperwork-driven gap ("social insurance should follow work, not labels"), and landed a real early hit by showing CON's 1099 point confuses annual tax reporting with the contemporaneous wage records eligibility actually runs on. PRO also answered the availability objection well by importing partial-unemployment machinery, and turned the capture argument neatly ("reporting confers no safe harbor; records arm misclassification plaintiffs") — a turn CON never squarely answered. But CON controlled the decisive axis: earnings records prove income, not involuntary loss. CON's 2020 emergency-program example (income was visible; the *reason* was not) went unanswered across two PRO speeches. CON then used PRO's own answer against it: when PRO named who actually collects (the deactivated, the app that exits a market), CON showed the ordinary way platform income falls — slow weeks, saturated zones, self-reduced hours — is precisely what the rules must deny, so the premium falls on students, retirees and second-jobbers who mostly never draw. PRO's "every pool has non-claimants" reply was then cleanly distinguished by CON's fire-insurance analogy (in a fire pool every member can claim), which PRO had no chance to rebut. CON also pointed out PRO's signature image — the driver hit by the van — is an injured, unavailable worker whom UI was never going to pay, exposing the framing as unreached by its own mechanism; PRO's broader "social-insurance" wording could have absorbed this but PRO had framed it as unemployment throughout and never repaired it. Both Q rounds were pointed and both sides used proper A1:/A2: labels; CON's demand that PRO commit against a classification safe harbor forced an honest refusal that CON then exploited plausibly (if somewhat speculatively). CON pays a real execution cost for two clipped turns, which trims the margin, but its comparative ledger — certain cost on the lowest earners, narrow uncertain benefit, adjudicated on data written by the payer — was the clearer reason to vote.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's use of PRO's own answer at [B4.2]: once PRO named deactivation and market exit as the claimable events, CON showed the mandate insures a narrow few while levying the many at the bottom, and then defused PRO's "all pools have non-claimants" reply with the fire-insurance distinction — every member of a fire pool can claim when their house burns, whereas here the ordinary mode of platform income loss is denied by design.</best_rebuttal>
